title: Corkscrew
prompt: A labelled teaching model of the page 43 winged corkscrew seats its frame over a corked bottle. Turn screws the helix into the cork and moves its central rack downward, raising both wing handles through the meshing pinion sectors at their pivots. Press wings pushes the handles down so their pinions lift the central rack, helix and cork, with the frame reacting against the bottle neck. Reverse unscrews the removed cork from the helix as specimen handling. See-through shows the central toothed rack, two wing-mounted pinion sectors, wing pivots, frame, helix and cork. Do not put a central pinion between straight toothed arms.
blurb: A teaching adaptation of the page 43 winged corkscrew uses two wing-mounted pinion sectors to lift a central rack, helix and cork.
adaptation: Source-supported rack-and-pinion extraction with staged operator specimen handling and reset, not an exact reconstruction.
truthNotes: The central toothed rack meshes with two pinion sectors integral with the wing handles.
The frame foot bears on the bottle lip while the cork lifts.
Reverse first moves the tool and cork clear of the neck, then represents a held cork moving down the reversed helix.
Reset is specimen exchange by the operator.
Teeth are simplified trapezoidal teaching profiles.
1988 is inaccessible and unverified. No edition-union claim.

identity.note: Gears and Belts / The Rack and Pinion / Corkscrew and Removing a Cork, page 43 in both editions.
identity.mechanism: The helix screws into the cork as the central rack descends and the wing handles rise. Pressing the handles down rotates their pinion sectors and lifts the rack, helix and cork against the bottle-neck support.
identity.classificationNote: Only The Wheel and Axle and Gears and Belts are main principle chapters in this unit. Other entries are named examples, diagrams or subsection headings. Greek Mill has both historical context and a named mechanism diagram.

adaptationDecision.reason: Retain. It is a specific rack-and-pinion and screw application. The earlier bottle opener uses simple lever action on a cap and sardine key winds a band. The generic rack rig supplies the principle, not this extraction sequence.
adaptationDecision.boundary: Catalog and figure metadata establish intended scope only. No existing figure runtime was certified.

prompt.note: Actions are faithful but the parts list is wrong or too ambiguous. The source places pinions on the long handles and a rack on the central moving stem. It does not show one central pinion driving toothed straight arms. Correct that allocation explicitly.
prompt.apparatusRelation: Named winged extraction mechanism with staged specimen handling. The helix and rack work in sequence rather than becoming extra unsourced machine options.

builderTruthNotes: Simple compound tool. Real frame, two wings, pivots, pinion sectors, central rack, helix, handle, cork and bottle neck suffice.

Label all meaningful drawn real components and physical features. Distinguish force and travel overlays from anatomy. The individual builder brief must declare its expected minimum before building. No invented parts to meet a quota.
Identify the teaching adaptation in metadata, blurb and truth notes. Reset, specimen exchange, slow view and hand positioning are teaching controls rather than hidden machine hardware.
